title: Everyday voices deserve a place in the archive
excerpt: A community archive should make room for everyday experience, not only famous names and major events.
body: This editorial note invites contributors to document everyday experiences: learning a language at home, remembering a village, practising a craft, teaching songs, or describing how community life changes. Share each account with consent.

title: Remembering places through family stories
excerpt: Family memories can help younger generations ask better questions about the places they belong to.
body: Ask relatives what a place was called, how people travelled, what work shaped the seasons and which memories they wish to pass on. Record different accounts without forcing them into one single version.

title: The Asur Legend — how Sing Bonga outwitted the iron-smelters
contributor: Traditional tale · recorded by S. C. Roy (1912)
excerpt: The best-loved of the old Munda legends: the Asurs whose furnaces scorched the earth, the boy with the itching sores who was Sing Bonga in disguise, and how the bongas of hill and forest came to be.

image.caption: Hill and forest country of the Chota Nagpur plateau — the landscape of the Asur legend.
image.credit: Photo: Dev0745 · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Long ago, the Asurs — a people whose craft was smelting iron — worked their furnaces day and night without rest. The heat dried up the streams, tanks and pools, and scorched all the vegetation of the earth, until the beasts came and complained to Sing Bonga, the Sun-God, the supreme deity of the Mundas.
The messengers

Sing Bonga first thought of slaying the Asurs, but his consort counselled cunning instead. He sent the Dingchua and the Kerketa birds with an order: the furnaces were to be worked only by day, or only by night. The Asurs laughed at the messengers and smeared them with coal-dust and iron-ore dust — which is why those birds are black and grey to this day. Golden and silver vultures sent after them were beaten with hammer and iron pincers, and the Lipo and the Kuhu were driven away the same way.
The boy with the itching sores

Then Sing Bonga came down to earth in disguise — as the Toro Kora, a boy covered in itching sores — and took shelter in the house of the old couple Lutkum Haram and Lutkum Buria, guarding their drying grain from the fowls. Playing guli and kati — marbles and pickets — against twelve Asur boys and thirteen Deota boys, the boy's gulis of eggs and katis of rice-cakes smashed the iron ones of his opponents to pieces.

In those days the Asurs' furnaces began to fail. Divination with the sup, the winnowing fan, pointed to the Toro Kora, and reading the rice-grains he prescribed sacrifices in turn — a white fowl, then a white goat, then a young sheep. Each restored the furnaces only for a little while. At last he declared that a human sacrifice was required. The Asurs tried to buy a Munda child, but the Munda parents scorned the offer — so the Toro Kora offered himself. Before going, he consoled the old couple with a promise: he would establish the Pahan's son under a tree in the middle of the village, to offer sacrifices for them at the Baha flower feast, at Batauli, and at the Mage feast.
The treasure in the furnace

Two fasting virgins worked new bellows for three days and nights. And when the furnace was opened, the boy stepped out radiant as the morning sun, covered in gold and silver, and carrying a precious plate and bowl. He told the greedy Asurs that far more treasure lay inside, hidden under the wings of a golden and a silver vulture — and that every man must go in together, so that none could rob another. When all the Asur men were inside, Sing Bonga ordered the women to plaster up the furnace, kindle the fire and work the bellows. Sounds came from within; the women were told the men were quarrelling over the spoils, and that the red liquid they saw was betel juice being spat out. When the furnace was opened at last, there was nothing inside but charred bones and ashes.
How the bongas came to be

Then Sing Bonga revealed himself. The Asur women he hurled to the mountains and rocks, the deep waters and uplands, the woods, springs, meadows and groves — there their spirits would dwell forever as bongas, the presiding deities of those places, to be consulted by the soothsayers through rice-grains and lamplight, and to receive offerings from the Pahan. So the legend explains, all at once, the bongas of hill and stream, the village priesthood of the Pahan, and the calling of the soothsayers.

Retold, without addition, from the text recorded by Sarat Chandra Roy in “The Mundas and Their Country” (1912), Appendix I — who calls this legend “first and foremost in point of sanctity and popularity” among the traditions of the Mundas. The same legend is also preserved in the Encyclopaedia Mundarica.

title: Karma and Dharma — the legend of Karam Raja
contributor: Traditional tale · recorded at Jojohatu (Census of India, 1961)
excerpt: The origin legend of the Karma festival, as told at Jojohatu: how dancing came down from Indra's heaven, how Karma lost everything the night he cut down the Karam branches, and how he crossed forest and river to find Karam Raja floating on the water.

image.caption: Karam (Karma) puja being celebrated in Jharkhand.
image.credit: Photo: Pankaj076 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: At Jojohatu, a Munda village in the Khunti hills, the Karma festival is kept for wealth, prosperity and pleasure in life — and this is the legend its people tell of how the festival began. It was recorded there by the Census of India in 1961. Like all such tales it exists in other versions in other villages; this is Jojohatu's own.
How dancing came to earth

In the early days, dancing was not known in this world. It lived only in the palace of King Indra in the heavens, where the parees — the nymphs — danced. In the palace there lived a bhaunra, a hornet, and his wife. One day the hornet found a beautiful flower and gave it to his wife, warning her never to show it to the nymphs. But she was so enamoured of the flower that she came down daily to fetch more from the garden of King Aja on earth — and one day, she showed it. The nymphs were desperate to have such flowers, and that evening they refused to dance.

So Indra, the nymphs and the hornet rode down in Indra's chariot to King Aja's garden and plucked the flowers — and it became their daily practice. At last the gardener detected the theft and told the king, who had a special ash, treated with magic, sprayed upon the flowers. That night the chariot and the nymphs were caught fast, motionless, unable to return to heaven. Indra explained himself: the flowers decorated the nymphs when they performed the Karma dance, the source of all the wealth and prosperity of his kingdom, and he advised King Aja to perform the dance too. But the chariot could move again, Aja said, only if touched by a virgin girl who had fasted that day. Such a girl was found — a widow's daughter, who that very morning had quarrelled with her mother, so that neither had cooked or eaten. She touched the chariot, Indra returned to heaven, and from that day King Aja performed the Karma dance and grew from wealth to greater wealth. The art of dancing had come to earth.
Karma's journey for salt

King Aja had two sons, Anayashri and Danyashri, who were the fathers of Karma and Dharma. In those days salt was scarce in the kingdom, and on Indra's advice Karma was sent to Katak to bring salt. Merchant after merchant refused him, until at last one big businessman sold him a large stock, and Karma came home with it loaded on bullock carts. Nearing the village, he sent a messenger ahead to Dharma, asking to be received properly after his long journey. But Dharma was engaged in the worship of the Karma god, and sent back word: wait. A second messenger brought the same answer.

Enraged, Karma went himself to his brother's place, leaving the carts behind — and in his fury he cut down all the Karam branches, destroyed the articles of worship, and quarrelled with Dharma. That night the brothers parted. Karma went back for his salt and found the bullock carts all empty. At home his building stood in ruins, and his wife and children were in rags, and hungry.
The empty carts

Karma went to Dharma's house, where delicious dishes were being served to the guests, as is usual after the Karma festival. He was asked to wait — guests must have precedence over family. He went again, and was met with the same reply. In despair he took his wife and children to work in Dharma's fields; and when the day's work was done and he asked for his wages, Dharma gave wages first to the outside labourers, and only after them to Karma, who was but a member of the family. Enraged a second time, Karma went back to the field and began uprooting all the seedlings he had transplanted. But as fast as he tore them out, a beautiful man was transplanting them again. The man told him to worship Karam Raja — for all his troubles had come from his own bad Karam, his luck.
In search of Karam Raja

So Karma set out in search of Karam Raja. On the way he met a tortoise hanging from the branch of a tree in great pain, and it begged him to pray before Karam Raja for its salvation. Further on he met a woman with a borsi — a small earthen pot used as a hearth — fixed upon her head, and she made the same request. Then he came to a tank full of insects, where a crocodile lay with a big palm tree growing above its body, and it too asked Karma to pray for it.

At last Karma saw Karam Raja floating in a river. He jumped into the water to touch the deity's feet, but because of his sin he could not reach them. For hours he tried, until, dejected and exhausted, he was on the point of sinking. Then Karam Raja took pity on him and saved him. Karma prayed, and all his troubles were over: his lost wealth and prosperity returned to him. And he did not forget the others — he prayed for the tortoise, the woman and the crocodile, and they too were relieved of their sufferings. From that very day, the legend says, people began to have great faith in the Karma festival, and to perform it with zeal and enthusiasm.

In Jojohatu's own account, the festival is observed on the eleventh day of Bhado (August–September), in a household where the Ojha has advised it — sometimes after a shoot, an “ankoor”, appears in the paddy. Virgin girls bring baskets of earth from the field and the Karam god is installed in clay in the courtyard; bachelors cut two Bhelwa branches in the forest, and the branches are planted and worshipped with flowers. No sacrifice of any kind is permitted; handia, rice beer, is freely used, and the dancing goes on all night and from door to door the next day. The festival is performed every alternate year, for it is believed that in the year between, the Karam god goes to visit his other relatives.
Retold, without addition, from the legend recorded in “Jojohatu, a Munda Village” — Census of India 1961, Village Survey Monograph (Khunti Subdivision, District Ranchi), published 1963.
